Credit Mobilier. The scandal that revealed how a shell company could funnel millions in stolen profits straight into the hands of congressmen and government officials.

It started with the Union Pacific Railroad. In the mid-1860s, the railroad's directors, led by Thomas C. Durant, created a construction company called Credit Mobilier of America. This wasn't just a normal contractor. It was their way of siphoning money from the railroad itself. Between 1865 and 1869, Credit Mobilier charged the Union Pacific over 94 million dollars for work that was worth roughly 50 million. That's a 40 million dollar theft, spread across four years.

To keep Congress quiet and prevent any investigation, Credit Mobilier distributed free or cheap stock to prominent congressmen and senators, along with members of the Grant administration. It was outright bribery through stock options.

The scheme fell apart in 1872 when Henry C. Adams, a reporter for the New York Sun, exposed the entire operation. Thomas W. Knox pursued the story relentlessly. Congressional investigations followed, and two men became the public faces of the scandal. Representative Oakes Ames and Senator James W. Patterson had both distributed the stock, and they were formally censured by Congress.

The railroad was finished in 1869, and the country finally had its transcontinental route. But the scandal did real damage. It destroyed public confidence in both government and corporate accountability. The affair became emblematic of Gilded Age corruption and sparked later reforms in railroad regulation and congressional ethics. The scandal's reach extended beyond just the railroad men too. Ulysses S. Grant was president when these bribes were being distributed to his administration. Thomas C. Durant orchestrated the whole scheme. And the transcontinental railroad itself, though it was completed, became forever tainted by the corruption that had funded it.
